transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15 10:00 PT; Duration: ~62 minutes; Location: Zoom; Recording: yes
Attendees: Ethan, Alyssa, Marco, Priya, Samira, Leah, Jon, Harold, Samantha

Summary (auto): go over scheduling shim and define who owns fallback for launch.
Topics: scheduling shim, fallback ownership, kv cache, canaries

00:00 Ethan: okay let's kick off, we want to be deliberate about the scheduling shim semantics, I'm seeing some confusion between runtime and routing layers
00:18 Alyssa: yeah, sorry, quick context — product wants two knobs: latency-preferred and cost-preferred, and the shim should respect both but not create thrashing
00:34 Marco: right, and to be clear, the shim is in the serving proxy, not the routing plane, so there is a little bit of overlap with routing policies, that's where we've seen the previous accident where requests got bounced between pods
00:52 Priya: and in that case the KV cache warmed per pod so you lost the prefix cache, which spiked token latency — I keep hearing people say K V cash, ha
01:10 Samira: yeah transcription is going to say K V cash, we should call that out, KV cache.
01:20 Leah: can we capture the exact failure mode? like, what sequence triggers the fallback from dedicated to hosted?
01:33 Ethan: good Q. Walkthrough: routing policy checks capacity tier, if not available it selects variant model x-small which is quantized; shim decides whether to batch or not based on latency target. The conflict arises when routing reroutes to a different cluster and shim decides to queue for batching — then the requesting client times out
01:58 Jon: timeline — clients have 3s client-side timeout for chat. If shim batches for 400ms but routing reassigns, we saw end-to-end 4.2s last time.
02:18 Harold: and that's the gap we need to own — who is responsible for preempting batching when cross-cluster fallback happens?
02:35 Alyssa: product wants that to be preemptive in routing; runtime should expose a cancel hook. So routing can signal 'do not batch, immediate' on fallback paths
02:52 Marco: technical note: we can implement a fast-cancel on the runtime side by adding an early-exit flag in the batch scheduling loop, but we need a consistent wire-level signal — maybe a header X-Redwood-Fallback: true
03:14 Priya: if we add that header we also need to ensure it doesn't explode cardinality in our metrics ingestion; Samira and I had a problem with high-metric labels last quarter
03:30 Samira: suggest we use a boolean header and map it to an enum in metrics, not free-form strings. Also annotate traces so we can see when the shim aborted a batch
03:44 Ethan: good. Next — ownership. If it's a routing decision that triggers a fallback, routing owns the decision but runtime owns graceful cancellation and metric instrumentation
03:58 Alyssa: will capture that in the playbook: routing = decision, runtime = execution + observability. Ops (oncall) = mitigation + rollback authority
04:15 Samantha (Head of Reliability): and oncall must have clear steps — if variant fallback triggers high error rate, what's the atomic rollback? Do we pin to a previous model or divert traffic regionally?
04:32 Harold: capacity wise we may want to divert to dedicated pool in same region before we start model swapping across regions; that's cheaper than cold start region-move
04:47 Jon: can we define the SLO thresholds where routing will try dedicated vs swap models? We need a table of thresholds
05:02 Marco: I started a draft table in the routing policy doc, will link — it includes CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, and tail-latency thresholds
05:15 Alyssa: action: Marco attach that table and add the decision matrix row for client timeouts (3s typical)
05:28 Ethan: ok scenario walkthrough — I have three: A) KV eviction storm during a canary B) Cross-cluster routing fallback during peak Batches C) Autoscaler race where scale-up lags behind warmup
05:45 Priya: let's do A first. In A, we hit a pattern where many small prefix tokens increased cache thrash. We saw memory pressure cause eviction and subsequent latency spike.
06:01 Samira: the mitigation we prototyped was prefix-KV sticky routing — keep a request's affinity to a small pool where its prefix cache is warm. But that reduces overall packing
06:16 Leah: product asks for a hybrid — prefer affinity for low-latency chat sessions, but not for batch jobs. Can shim tag sessions as interactive vs batch?
06:31 Marco: yes we have session metadata in the proxy. We can set affinity TTLs. The trade-off is lower GPU utilization for sticky sessions, but net latency improves for PLG experience
06:48 Alyssa: put that in the decisions doc: interactive = affinity 60s, batch = no affinity.
06:59 Ethan: onto B: cross-cluster fallback. We saw the scrambling last release when one region's pool hit an OOM and routing switched to another region — but runtime kept batching causing increased latency
07:18 Priya: rehearsal — when fallback happens, routing will set X-Redwood-Fallback header, runtime will cancel pending batches, immediately flush small batches. If client-level timeout is smaller than flush, routing should prefer model variant within same region first
07:35 Jon: minor detail — clients sometimes set their own timeouts. We can't rely on them. We should add per-route timeout overrides in the control plane to enforce minimums
07:52 Marco: agreed, control plane can inject enforced timeouts at ingress; that avoids client variability
08:10 Samira: and we need trace sampling for these fallbacks. Right now we only sample 1% which hides tail behaviors; increase to 10% for fallback flagged requests temporarily
08:26 Priya: note on metrics — create a fallback-rate metric and an eviction-spike metric, both with tags: route, region, model_variant
08:42 Ethan: good. C: autoscaler race. We saw that when scale-up took 30s and warmup another 40s, requests spilled to fallback variants — we need a safety 'burst' capacity reserve for canaries/PLG spikes
08:58 Harold: capacity can reserve a 5% burst pool per region for critical routes. It costs money but reduces user-visible failures
09:14 Alyssa: product asks for an opt-in annotation on route to consume burst-reserve. We'll document which routes get it by default (chat-critical: true)
09:32 Leah: question: who flips the flag during rollout? The release engineer or product?
09:40 Ethan: release engineer flips during canary; product can request default change at the route-level
09:51 Priya: let's talk runbook rehearsal — when fallback rate > 2% for 10m, oncall runs the checklist. Checklist: 1) check KV eviction graphs 2) check batch queue lengths 3) look at routing decision table 4) if sustained, pin model variant or divert to dedicated pool
10:18 Jon: can we add the commands in runbook for quick pin? Like CLI snippets: redwoodctl route pin --variant=quant-v2 --duration=30m
10:34 Marco: I'll add CLI snippets and example Grafana links.
10:41 Samantha: ops wants an escalation matrix: page oncall -> if not resolved in 15m, page engineering -> if not resolved in 45m, exec notification
10:55 Ethan: agreed. Now, action item assignment (we'll speak quickly).
11:05 Alyssa: I'll update the playbook then loop in Capacity and Product.
11:12 Marco: prototype scheduling shim toggle pushed to branch shim-toggle by Friday, link in chat.
11:22 Priya: I'll run 48 hour KV eviction sim. Will run two configs: affinity on/off and eviction pressure.
11:35 Samira: canary plan — I'll draft a canary where 5% of traffic hits a route that forces a fallback path and we observe telemetry
11:44 Ethan: good. One last operational note: expose a metric that shows 'shim-cancel-rate' so we can correlate with fallback events
11:58 Alyssa: I'll add that to metrics list.
12:07 Leah: small ask — can we have a one-pager for execs describing the trade-offs? We don't need the deep tech detail, just outcomes and cost delta to hold burst capacity
12:18 Harold: I'll put numbers for 5% burst cost estimate by EOD tomorrow
12:25 Ethan: ok let's wrap. Next sync 2026-03-23 09:30 PT, priya will present eviction sim results, Marco will show shim toggle demo
12:40 End meeting.
